To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) 16 novel SOD1 gene point mutations have been discovered in ALS; 2) these mutations are not clustered within any particular part of the SOD1 coding sequence; 3) patients with SOD 1 mutations may infrequent show symptoms and signs not related to the motor systems; 4) the nature of the toxic function of mutant superoxide dismutases in ALS remains unresolved.
148/2045 (7.2%) ALS patients carried a SOD1 gene mutation and 16 novel SOD1 gene exonic mutations were found.
148 of 2045 ALS patients carried a disease associated mutation in the SODE1 gene, 16 of the 148 were novel mutations and the most prevalent was the 41% A4V mutation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of new mutations in the Cu,Zn superoxide dismtase gene (SOD1), and with the characterization of the phenotypic features of patients who carry these mutations.
the molecular basis of ALS.
the identification of novel mutations in the SOD-1 gene, which is associated with familial amyotrophic lateral scelerosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

mutations in SOD1 are a cause of familial ALS, and that SOD1 gene analysis may be a useful diagnostic tool in patients suspected of having ALS, especially in the presence of a family history of ALS or other motor neuron disorders.
the clinical phenotype of SOD1 mutations is highly variable and may be difficult to predict from the mutation alone.
the SOD1 mutations are not associated with a specific disease phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the clinical spectrum of SOD1 mutations is broad, and that the clinical features may vary from patient to patient with the same SOD1 mutation.
SOD1 mutations are a heterogeneous group of mutations, with no common structural or clinical denominator.
the SOD1 mutations are found both in familial and sporadic cases, without any definite predication for any part of SOD1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SOD1 mutations in ALS are heterogeneous and that no single mutation is more frequent than others.
SOD1 mutations can present with a wide range of clinical phenotypes and that it is not always possible to predict the phenotype based on the type of SOD1 mutation.
SOD1 testing in suspected ALS patients is a valuable diagnostic tool and that the clinical features of patients with different SOD1 gene variants are heterogeneous.
